body:
Reflection of incoming solar radiation

Not all incoming solar radiation is absorbed by the Earth–atmosphere system. Clouds, atmospheric particles and the Earth's surface reflect or scatter part of it back into space.

Albedo is the fraction or percentage of incoming radiation reflected by a surface or system.

In the study of climate, albedo commonly refers to the reflection of incoming solar radiation. A surface with high albedo reflects a larger fraction of the sunlight it receives, while a surface with low albedo generally absorbs a larger fraction, provided transmission is negligible.

For example, a surface that reflects 80 out of 100 units of incoming solar radiation has an albedo of 80%, or 0.8.

Relative albedo of different surfaces

  • Fresh snow generally has very high albedo.
  • Bright ice and light-coloured dry surfaces generally reflect more sunlight than dark surfaces.
  • Dark forests and asphalt commonly have relatively low albedo.
  • Water often has relatively low albedo when the Sun is high, but its reflectivity increases substantially at low solar angles.
  • Cloud albedo varies with cloud thickness, composition and other conditions.

The planetary albedo of Earth includes reflection and scattering by the atmosphere, clouds and the surface. It is approximately 30% in broad modern estimates, although its actual value varies.

Meaning of the global heat budget

The Earth's heat budget describes the balance between solar energy received and energy returned to space by the Earth–atmosphere system.

At the top of the atmosphere, the fundamental relationship is between absorbed solar radiation and outgoing longwave radiation. If these are equal over a sufficiently long period, the system has no net radiative energy gain or loss.

If absorbed solar radiation exceeds outgoing longwave radiation, the system gains energy. If outgoing longwave radiation exceeds absorbed solar radiation, it loses energy.

The 100-unit textbook heat budget

A simplified school-level model represents the incoming solar energy at the top of the atmosphere as 100 units. The following figures form the conventional NCERT heat-budget illustration:

Disposition of incoming solar energyUnits
Scattered back into space6
Reflected by clouds27
Reflected by the Earth's surface2
Absorbed by the atmosphere14
Absorbed by the Earth's surface51

The reflected and scattered components total 35 units. The atmosphere and surface together absorb the remaining 65 units.

Return of absorbed energy to space

In the same simplified accounting model, the surface transfers its 51 absorbed units through the following pathways:

  • 17 units of longwave radiation escape directly to space.
  • 6 units are transferred to the atmosphere through net radiative exchange.
  • 9 units are transferred through convection and turbulence.
  • 19 units are transferred through latent heat associated with evaporation and condensation.

The atmosphere receives 14 units directly from incoming solar radiation and 34 units through energy transfer from the surface. It emits a corresponding 48 units to space in this simplified model.

Thus, 17 units emitted directly from the surface and 48 units emitted by the atmosphere together return 65 units as longwave radiation. Along with the 35 reflected units, the total returned to space is 100 units.

Different textbook accounting models

The numerical partition varies between simplified educational illustrations. The Gujarat Standard 11 model also uses 35 reflected units but assigns 18 units to atmospheric absorption and 47 units to surface absorption.

Both models demonstrate the same basic principle: the incoming energy is partitioned between reflection, absorption and eventual energy loss to space. The numerical values belong to their respective simplified illustrations and should not be combined.

The 35-unit reflected fraction in these school diagrams is an illustrative accounting value. It is not an exact or permanently fixed measurement of modern planetary albedo. Similarly, global energy balance does not mean that the Earth can never undergo warming or cooling.

Ice–albedo feedback

Snow and ice reflect a large fraction of incoming sunlight. When they melt and expose darker land or ocean surfaces, the underlying surfaces generally absorb more solar energy.

The additional absorption can increase warming and promote further melting. This reinforcing process is called the ice–albedo feedback, an example of positive climatic feedback.

Prelims focus

  • Albedo refers to the reflected fraction of incoming radiation.
  • Fresh snow generally has higher albedo than dark land or water.
  • The NCERT model assigns 35 units to reflection, 14 to atmospheric absorption and 51 to surface absorption.
  • The Gujarat Standard 11 model assigns 35, 18 and 47 units respectively.
  • At radiative equilibrium, absorbed solar energy equals outgoing longwave energy.
  • Trap: Reflected shortwave radiation and emitted longwave radiation are different forms of energy transfer.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Heat Budget of the Planet Earth, p. 69, Figure 8.2; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 9, Temperature, p. 63, Figure 9.2; NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget, 2009, consulted 28 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Relative albedo of common natural and artificial surfaces.

pictures.alt: Energy flow from 100 solar units through reflection, surface and atmosphere, returning 35 reflected units and 65 longwave units to space.

title: Albedo and the Global Heat Budget

body:
Global balance does not mean local balance

The Earth–atmosphere system may approach an overall energy balance, but this does not mean that every latitude receives and loses equal amounts of radiation.

Low latitudes generally receive more solar energy because sunlight strikes them at relatively high angles. High latitudes generally receive less annual solar energy because the rays are more oblique and winter daylight is limited.

Outgoing longwave radiation also varies geographically, but its latitudinal variation differs from that of absorbed solar radiation.

Regions of radiative surplus and deficit

A region has a radiative surplus when it absorbs more solar energy than it emits as longwave radiation. A radiative deficit exists when outgoing longwave radiation exceeds absorbed solar radiation.

In the conventional annual-average geographical model, the region extending approximately from 40° N to 40° S has a net radiative surplus. Regions poleward of these approximate latitudes generally have a net radiative deficit.

The transition latitudes are not fixed geographical boundaries. They vary with season and the actual distribution of clouds, temperatures, ice and other atmospheric and surface conditions.

Redistribution through atmospheric circulation

Unequal heating produces differences in temperature, density and atmospheric pressure. These differences contribute to large-scale atmospheric circulation.

Moving air transports energy horizontally through advection. Water vapour also transports latent heat from regions of evaporation to regions where condensation occurs.

Atmospheric circulation therefore transfers part of the low-latitude energy surplus towards higher latitudes.

Redistribution through ocean currents

Ocean currents also transport considerable quantities of heat. Warm currents generally carry thermal energy away from lower latitudes, while colder currents return cooler water towards lower latitudes as part of the broader ocean circulation.

The warm Gulf Stream and its continuation into the North Atlantic contribute to the transport of tropical and subtropical heat towards higher northern latitudes.

Importance for the climate system

Without atmospheric and oceanic heat redistribution, the temperature contrast between low and high latitudes would be much greater.

Heat transport helps prevent the continual accumulation of excess energy in tropical regions and compensates for part of the radiative deficit in higher latitudes.

This does not make temperatures uniform. A temperature gradient between the equator and the poles remains an important feature of the climate system and helps sustain atmospheric and oceanic circulation.

Insolation supplies energy unevenly, while atmospheric and oceanic circulation redistribute that energy. The Earth's heat budget must therefore be understood together with geographical heat transport.

Prelims focus

  • Radiative surplus occurs when absorbed solar radiation exceeds outgoing longwave radiation.
  • Radiative deficit is the reverse condition.
  • The conventional annual-average surplus belt extends approximately between 40° N and 40° S.
  • Atmospheric circulation and ocean currents transport heat towards higher latitudes.
  • Trap: Global radiative balance does not require every individual latitude to be in local radiative balance.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Variation in the Net Heat Budget at the Earth's Surface, p. 70, Figure 8.3; NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget, 2009, consulted 28 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The belt from approximately 40° N to 40° S has radiative surplus; higher latitudes have deficits, with air and oceans carrying heat poleward.
pictures.caption: Latitudinal energy imbalance and poleward heat transport.

title: Latitudinal Heat Balance and Redistribution of Energy

body:
Temperature as an atmospheric element

Temperature measures the thermal condition of a substance and indicates how hot or cold it is. Atmospheric temperature is influenced by the amount of energy received, the amount lost and the transfer of energy from other regions.

Two places receiving similar insolation may have different air temperatures because of differences in altitude, water availability, surface properties, wind or proximity to the sea.

Latitude and altitude

Latitude

Low latitudes generally receive more concentrated annual solar radiation than high latitudes. Consequently, average surface air temperatures generally decrease towards the poles.

However, latitude is not the only control. High-altitude tropical locations can be cooler than low-altitude locations at greater latitudes.

Altitude

Air temperature generally decreases with altitude in the troposphere. This explains why hill stations often experience cooler conditions than nearby lowlands.

Saputara in Gujarat's Dang district is an example of a hill station whose elevated location contributes to its comparatively cool climate.

Distance from the sea and continentality

Land generally heats and cools more rapidly than large water bodies. The difference arises from several physical characteristics of water:

  • Water has a high specific heat capacity, so a given amount of energy produces a relatively small temperature change.
  • Water movement distributes absorbed heat through a greater depth.
  • Sunlight can penetrate beneath the water surface.
  • Evaporation removes substantial energy from water surfaces.

Over land, much of the absorbed solar energy heats a relatively shallow surface layer. Land temperatures can therefore rise and fall rapidly.

Maritime influence refers to the moderating effect of nearby large water bodies. Coastal regions generally experience smaller daily and annual temperature ranges.

Continentality refers to the stronger seasonal and daily temperature contrasts commonly experienced in regions located far from the moderating influence of the sea.

In Gujarat, coastal locations such as Veraval experience maritime influence from the Arabian Sea, whereas inland locations such as Ahmedabad are more exposed to continental temperature contrasts. Other local geographical factors also affect their climates.

Ocean currents and air masses

Warm and cold ocean currents modify coastal temperatures. The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift contribute to the relative warmth of western Europe, whereas the cold Labrador Current contributes to cooler conditions along parts of northeastern North America.

Air masses and winds can also alter local temperature. Warm-air advection increases temperatures, while cold-air advection decreases them. Cold waves and hot summer winds illustrate this effect.

Cloud cover, vegetation and surface characteristics

Cloud cover commonly reduces daytime solar heating and nighttime radiative cooling. Vegetation provides shade and supports evaporative cooling through transpiration. Moist surfaces generally use more energy in evaporation than dry surfaces, reducing the energy available for direct sensible heating.

Surface albedo, soil moisture and heat-storage capacity also influence temperature. Dark surfaces commonly absorb more sunlight than light-coloured surfaces under otherwise similar conditions.

Slope and aspect

The direction in which a slope faces is called its aspect. A slope facing the Sun generally receives more direct solar radiation than a slope facing away from it.

In northern mid-latitudes, south-facing slopes are generally warmer than comparable north-facing slopes. The opposite relationship commonly occurs in southern mid-latitudes. This rule must be applied carefully in tropical regions because the Sun can lie to either side of the zenith during different seasons.

Daily temperature variation

Solar radiation generally reaches its maximum intensity around local solar noon under clear conditions. However, surface air temperature commonly reaches its daily maximum later in the afternoon because the surface continues to gain energy for some time after noon.

The minimum temperature commonly occurs around sunrise or shortly afterwards, following a night of continuing radiative heat loss.

The diurnal temperature range is the difference between the highest and lowest temperatures recorded during a day.

If a location records a daily maximum of 38°C and a minimum of 20°C, its diurnal temperature range is 18°C.

Dry deserts often experience large diurnal temperature ranges because clear skies permit strong daytime heating and rapid nighttime cooling. Humid coastal and cloudy regions commonly experience smaller daily ranges.

Prelims focus

  • Latitude and altitude are distinct controls of air temperature.
  • Water heats and cools more slowly than land.
  • Continental interiors generally have larger temperature ranges than coastal areas.
  • Warm and cold currents influence coastal temperatures.
  • Daily maximum temperature usually occurs after solar noon.
  • Trap: Maximum insolation and maximum air temperature do not necessarily occur at the same time.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Factors Controlling Temperature Distribution, pp. 70–71; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapters 8 and 9, pp. 57–58, 64–65; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 4, Climate, Factors Determining the Climate of India.]
